algorithms.title: Kadane's Algorithm (Maximum Subarray Sum)
algorithms.summary: Finds the contiguous subarray with the maximum sum in a 1D array in linear O(N) time.
explanation: Maintain two variables: `currMax` (sum of current subarray) and `maxSoFar` (global maximum sum).
Iterate through the array. For each element `x`, add it to `currMax`.
If `currMax` becomes negative, reset `currMax = 0` (starting a fresh subarray from next element).
Update `maxSoFar = max(maxSoFar, currMax)` at each step.
To handle all-negative arrays, initialize `maxSoFar` with the first element or negative infinity.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds the contiguous sequence of numbers in an array that has the largest combined sum.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When asked for maximum continuous subarray sum or maximum profit window in single-pass array problems.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Financial stock portfolio maximum gain calculation, image processing signal peak detection, genomic sequence alignment scoring.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Reduces brute-force O(N³) or O(N²) nested loops to single linear scan O(N) with O(1) extra space.

codeTemplates.code:
def max_subarray_sum(nums):
    max_so_far = nums[0]
    curr_max = nums[0]
    
    for i in range(1, len(nums)):
        curr_max = max(nums[i], curr_max + nums[i])
        max_so_far = max(max_so_far, curr_max)
        
    return max_so_far

algorithms.title: Dutch National Flag Algorithm (Sort 0s, 1s, 2s)
algorithms.summary: Sorts an array containing only three distinct elements (e.g. 0s, 1s, 2s) in a single pass with O(1) space.
explanation: Maintain three pointers: `low` (boundary for 0s), `mid` (current element scanner), `high` (boundary for 2s).
Initially `low = 0`, `mid = 0`, `high = n - 1`.
Loop while `mid <= high`:
- If `arr[mid] == 0`: swap `arr[low]` & `arr[mid]`, then `low++`, `mid++`.
- If `arr[mid] == 1`: just `mid++`.
- If `arr[mid] == 2`: swap `arr[mid]` & `arr[high]`, then `high--` (do NOT increment mid yet).

traceSteps: Step 1: nums[mid] = 2. Swap nums[mid] and nums[high] (swap 2 & 0). Array = [0, 0, 2, 1, 1, 2], high = 4.
Step 2: nums[mid] = 0. Swap nums[low] and nums[mid] (swap 0 & 0). low = 1, mid = 1. Array = [0, 0, 2, 1, 1, 2].
Step 3: nums[mid] = 0. Swap nums[low] and nums[mid] (swap 0 & 0). low = 2, mid = 2. Array = [0, 0, 2, 1, 1, 2].
Step 4: nums[mid] = 2. Swap nums[mid] and nums[high] (swap 2 & 1). Array = [0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2], high = 3.
Step 5: nums[mid] = 1. mid++. mid = 3, low = 2, high = 3. Array = [0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2].
Step 6: nums[mid] = 1. mid++. mid = 4 > high (3). Loop terminates.
Result array is sorted in O(N) time with 0 extra memory: [0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2].

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Sorts a 3-valued array in-place without using extra counting arrays or multi-pass sorting algorithms.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When an array contains 3 unique key values (e.g. 0/1/2, Red/White/Blue, Low/Medium/High risk tags).
wAnswers.whereUsed: Partitioning elements in QuickSort pivot steps, multi-class classification bucket sorting in memory managers.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Guarantees exact O(N) time with only 3 pointers and zero memory allocation.

algorithms.title: Boyer-Moore Majority Voting Algorithm (Majority Element > N/2)
algorithms.summary: Finds the majority element that appears more than N/2 times in an array in single pass O(N) time and O(1) space.
explanation: Initialize `candidate = None` and `count = 0`.
Iterate through the array. For each element `x`:
- If `count == 0`, set `candidate = x` and `count = 1`.
- Else if `x == candidate`, increment `count++`.
- Else, decrement `count--`.
The remaining `candidate` is guaranteed to be the majority element if one exists.

traceSteps: Candidate = 2. Verification step counts occurrences of 2: 4 times (> 7/2). Verified output: 2.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds the element appearing strictly more than 50% of the time in linear time without hash maps.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When finding dominant element in a stream or array with frequency > N/2 or > N/3.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Consensus voting protocols in distributed systems, real-time telemetry anomaly filtering, stream processing.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Replaces Hash Map frequency count O(N) space with O(1) space and 1 linear pass.

algorithms.title: Next Permutation Algorithm (Lexicographical Order)
algorithms.summary: Rearranges numbers into the lexicographically next greater permutation in-place in linear O(N) time.
explanation: Step 1 (Find Break Point): Scan from right to left to find the first index `i` where `nums[i] < nums[i+1]`.
If no such index exists (array is strictly decreasing), reverse the whole array (first permutation).
Step 2 (Find Swap Target): Scan from right to left to find index `j` where `nums[j] > nums[i]`.
Step 3 (Swap): Swap `nums[i]` and `nums[j]`.
Step 4 (Reverse Suffix): Reverse the subarray from index `i+1` to end of array to get the smallest possible tail suffix.

traceSteps: Step 1: Traverse right-to-left to find first dip where nums[i] < nums[i+1]. Dip at index i = 1 (val = 3, since 3 < 5).
Step 2: Traverse right-to-left to find smallest number > nums[1] (3). Index j = 3 (val = 4, since 4 > 3).
Step 3: Swap nums[1] and nums[3] (swap 3 and 4). Array becomes [1, 4, 5, 3, 2].
Step 4: Reverse elements after index 1 (indices 2 to 4: [5, 3, 2] -> [2, 3, 5]).

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Generates the next lexicographical permutation of an array in-place without generating all N! permutations.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When asked for next permutation, next lexicographical number sequence, or TSP permutation search.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Combinatorial optimization solvers, permutation generators in C++ `std::next_permutation`, hardware test pattern sequence generator.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Replaces full DFS recursion generation O(N!) with O(N) single-pass in-place swap & reverse.

algorithms.title: Reversal Algorithm for Array Rotation
algorithms.summary: Rotates an array to the right or left by K steps in O(N) time and O(1) extra space using 3 reverse operations.
explanation: Normalize `k = k % n` (in case `k > n`).
To rotate right by K steps:
1. Reverse the entire array `[0...n-1]`.
2. Reverse the first K elements `[0...k-1]`.
3. Reverse the remaining elements `[k...n-1]`.
To rotate left by K steps: Reverse `[0...k-1]`, reverse `[k...n-1]`, then reverse entire array `[0...n-1]`.

traceSteps: Step 2: Reverse first k elements [7, 6, 5] (index 0 to 2) -> [5, 6, 7]. Array = [5, 6, 7, 4, 3, 2, 1].
Step 3: Reverse remaining n-k elements [4, 3, 2, 1] (index 3 to 6) -> [1, 2, 3, 4]. Array = [5, 6, 7, 1, 2, 3, 4].
Rotated array achieved in O(N) time and O(1) space.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Rotates elements in an array by K positions in-place without creating a temporary copy array.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When rotating arrays, cyclic shift operations, or ring buffer offset realignment.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Circular buffer memory management, GUI carousel item shift, CPU cache line rotation.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Achieves O(N) time and O(1) auxiliary space compared to naive cyclic shifts taking O(N * K) or O(N) space.

algorithms.title: Merge Overlapping Intervals Algorithm
algorithms.summary: Combines all overlapping intervals in an array of start-end pairs into non-overlapping ranges.
explanation: Sort intervals by start time `intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])`.
Initialize `merged = [intervals[0]]`.
For each interval `[start, end]` in sorted list:
- Get last interval in `merged`: `lastStart, lastEnd = merged[-1]`.
- If `start <= lastEnd` (overlap): merge by updating `merged[-1][1] = max(lastEnd, end)`.
- Else (no overlap): append `[start, end]` to `merged`.

traceSteps: Step 1: Sort intervals by start time -> [[1,3], [2,6], [8,10], [15,18]].
Step 2: Add first interval [1,3] to merged list.
Step 3: Process [2,6]: Start 2 <= Last end 3 -> Overlap! Merge: end = max(3, 6) = 6. Last interval becomes [1,6].
Step 4: Process [8,10]: Start 8 > Last end 6 -> No overlap! Add [8,10] to merged list.
Step 5: Process [15,18]: Start 15 > Last end 10 -> No overlap! Add [15,18] to merged list.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Consolidates overlapping time windows or numerical ranges into minimal disjoint sets.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When given calendar events, meeting rooms, IP range allocations, or line segment overlaps.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Google Calendar meeting clash detection, OS memory segment allocation, network CIDR range aggregation.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Sorting reduces interval comparison complexity from O(N²) to O(N log N) single pass.

algorithms.title: Prefix Sum & Difference Array Technique
algorithms.summary: Precomputes cumulative sum array to perform range sum queries [L, R] in O(1) constant time.
explanation: Precompute `prefix[i] = prefix[i-1] + arr[i]` with `prefix[0] = 0`.
Sum of range `[L, R]` is calculated instantly as `prefix[R + 1] - prefix[L]`.
Difference Array variant: To apply range addition `+V` to `[L, R]`, execute `diff[L] += V` and `diff[R + 1] -= V`. Take prefix sum at the end.

traceSteps: Step 1: Build Prefix Sum array P where P[i] = P[i-1] + nums[i].
Query answered in O(1) time complexity.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Answers multi-range sum queries in O(1) time and applies batch range update operations.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When querying subarray sums repeatedly or applying range updates (e.g. Subarray Sum Equals K, Car Pooling).
wAnswers.whereUsed: 2D Image integral images for face detection (Viola-Jones), audio loudness metering, database range aggregation.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Replaces O(N) range sum loops with O(1) single subtraction operation.

algorithms.title: Maximum Product Subarray (Kadane Variant)
algorithms.summary: Finds contiguous subarray with maximum product in O(N) time by tracking both current minimum and maximum products.
explanation: Since multiplying two negative numbers yields a positive number, a negative number can turn a minimum product into maximum!
Maintain `currMax` and `currMin` initialized to `nums[0]`.
For each element `x` from index 1:
- If `x < 0`: swap `currMax` and `currMin`.
- `currMax = max(x, currMax * x)`.
- `currMin = min(x, currMin * x)`.
- Update global `ans = max(ans, currMax)`.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds contiguous subarray with maximum multiplicative product handling negative numbers & zeros.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When multiplying elements in continuous subarray where negative signs flip product signs.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Compound interest gain optimization, financial risk model product series analysis.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Computes max product in single linear scan O(N) with O(1) space instead of O(N²) nested loops.

codeTemplates.code:
def maxProduct(nums):
    res = max(nums)
    curr_max = curr_min = 1
    for n in nums:
        if n == 0:
            curr_max = curr_min = 1
            continue
        tmp = curr_max * n
        curr_max = max(n * curr_max, n * curr_min, n)
        curr_min = min(tmp, n * curr_min, n)
        res = max(res, curr_max)
    return res

algorithms.title: Count Inversions in Array (Modified Merge Sort)
algorithms.summary: Counts pairs (i, j) such that i < j and arr[i] > arr[j] in O(N log N) time using Divide and Conquer.
explanation: An inversion pair indicates how far an array is from being sorted.
Modify Merge Sort during the `merge(left, right)` step.
When `arr[i] > arr[j]` (where `i` is in left half and `j` is in right half):
- All remaining elements in left half from `i` to `mid` are also greater than `arr[j]`!
- Add `(mid - i + 1)` to `inversion_count`.
Return total sum of inversions from left half, right half, and merge step.

traceSteps: Divide array into left [8, 4] and right [2, 1].
Merge [8] and [4]: 8 > 4 -> Inversion count += 1. Sorted left = [4, 8].
Merge [2] and [1]: 2 > 1 -> Inversion count += 1. Sorted right = [1, 2].
Compare left[0]=4 with right[0]=1: 4 > 1 -> Inversion count += remaining elements in left (2 elements: 4, 8). count = 2 + 2 = 4.
Compare left[0]=4 with right[1]=2: 4 > 2 -> Inversion count += remaining elements in left (2 elements: 4, 8). count = 4 + 2 = 6.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Measures how out-of-order an array is (number of swaps required to sort).
wAnswers.whenToUse: When asked for inversion count, similarity between two ranked lists, or 15-puzzle solvability test.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Recommendation engines (Collaborative Filtering preference similarity), Kendall tau distance calculation.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Reduces O(N²) pair comparison to O(N log N) using divide-and-conquer merge sort.

algorithms.title: Pascal's Triangle Algorithm (Combinatorics & Row Generation)
algorithms.summary: Generates Pascal's triangle where each element is the sum of two numbers directly above it.
explanation: Element at row `r` and column `c` (0-indexed) equals combination `nCr(r, c) = r! / (c! * (r - c)!)`.
To generate Row `R` in O(R) time: `val = val * (r - i) / i` iteratively.
To generate full Triangle up to N rows: Maintain 2D array where `row[i][j] = row[i-1][j-1] + row[i-1][j]` with edges = 1.

traceSteps: Generated Row 4 in O(N) time & O(1) auxiliary space: [1, 4, 6, 4, 1].

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Computes binomial coefficients, combinations `nCr`, and probability distribution matrices.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When finding combination values, grid unique paths, or polynomial expansion coefficients.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Binomial distribution calculations, Bezier curve rendering in computer graphics, combinatorics.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Generates Nth row in O(N) time without factorial integer overflow.

algorithms.title: KMP Algorithm (Knuth-Morris-Pratt Pattern Matching)
algorithms.summary: Efficiently finds pattern matches in a text string without re-checking matching characters using the Longest Proper Prefix which is also Suffix (LPS) table.
explanation: Precompute the `LPS` (Longest Prefix Suffix) array for the pattern of length M.
`LPS[i]` stores the length of the longest matching proper prefix of `pattern[0...i]` that is also a suffix of `pattern[0...i]`.
Scan the text of length N with index `i` and pattern with index `j`.
When characters match (`text[i] == pattern[j]`), advance both `i++` and `j++`.
When a mismatch occurs, use `LPS[j-1]` to skip redundant pattern comparisons instead of resetting `i` back.

traceSteps: Step 1: Compute LPS array for 'ABACABA' -> LPS = [0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 2, 3].
i=0..4: 'ABABA' matches 'ABABA', mismatch at text[5]='C' vs pattern[5]='B'.
Use LPS[4] = 1: shift pattern pointer j to 1. Match resumes.
Pattern matched at index 6 in O(N + M) linear time.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds exact occurrences of a pattern P of length M inside text T of length N in linear time.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When searching for substrings in huge text corpora, DNA sequence matching, or avoiding worst-case O(N * M) naive string matching.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Text editor search utilities (`grep`, Ctrl+F), genomic sequence search tools (BLAST), network packet filtering.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Eliminates backtracking in the primary text stream. Time complexity remains linear O(N + M) regardless of text repetitions.

algorithms.title: Rabin-Karp Algorithm (Polynomial Rolling Hash Matching)
algorithms.summary: Uses rolling hash techniques to find pattern matches in linear average time by maintaining a sliding hash value.
explanation: Compute the polynomial hash of the pattern of length M: hash(P) = sum(P[i] * B^(M-1-i)) % MOD.
Compute the initial hash of the first window of text of length M.
Slide the window over the text one character at a time:
- Subtract the outgoing character's contribution: (hash - text[old] * B^(M-1)) % MOD.
- Shift left: (hash * B) % MOD.
- Add the incoming character's contribution: (hash + text[new]) % MOD.
If the text window hash equals the pattern hash, perform a character-by-character comparison to handle hash collisions.

exampleTrace.input: text = 'GEEKS FOR GEEKS', pattern = 'GEEK', prime q = 101
exampleTrace.output: Pattern found at index 0 and index 10
traceSteps: Step 1: Calculate hash for pattern 'GEEK' = H_p.
Step 2: Calculate hash for first window text[0..3] 'GEEK' = H_w.
Step 3: Window 0: H_w == H_p. Character-by-character check matches 'GEEK' at index 0.
Step 4: Roll hash for window 1 text[1..4] 'EEKS': subtract 'G', multiply base, add 'S' mod 101.
Step 5: Continue rolling window hash until window 10 text[10..13] 'GEEK': H_w == H_p. Match at index 10.
Pattern matches found in O(N + M) average time.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds pattern occurrences in text and handles multiple pattern search efficiently using rolling hashes.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When searching for multiple patterns simultaneously, detecting duplicate substrings, or checking plagiarism.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Plagiarism detectors, virus signature scanning in antivirus software, DNA motif matching.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Recomputes substring hash in O(1) time per step instead of re-hashing from scratch O(M).

algorithms.title: Z-Algorithm (Linear Time Z-Array Pattern Search)
algorithms.summary: Constructs a Z-array where Z[i] is the length of the longest substring starting at i that matches the prefix of the concatenated string P + '$' + T.
explanation: Construct concatenated string S = pattern + '$' + text.
Maintain a Z-box [L, R] which is the segment of S matching a prefix of S with maximum right endpoint R.
For index i from 1 to len(S):
- If i > R: Compute Z[i] naively by comparing S[i+k] with S[k], then update [L, R] = [i, i + Z[i] - 1].
- If i <= R: Use previously computed Z[i - L]. If Z[i - L] < R - i + 1, then Z[i] = Z[i - L]. Otherwise extend naively beyond R and update [L, R].
Check indices where Z[i] == len(pattern) to find exact match positions.

exampleTrace.output: Z-array computed, Pattern matched where Z[i] == len(pattern)
traceSteps: i=4 (first 'a' of T): S[4..6]='aab' matches prefix S[0..2]='aab' -> Z[4] = 3 (length of pattern 'aab')!
Since Z[4] == len('aab') == 3, pattern 'aab' is matched at text index 0.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds all occurrences of a pattern in a text in O(N + M) time and finds longest common prefixes.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When needing linear time pattern matching, finding period of a string, or prefix-suffix overlaps.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Bioinformatics DNA sequence alignment, text editor search engines, string compression algorithms.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Reuses previously calculated prefix match bounds [L, R] to process each character in O(1) amortized time.

algorithms.title: Manacher's Algorithm (Longest Palindromic Substring in O(N))
algorithms.summary: Finds the longest palindromic substring in linear time O(N) by transforming the string to handle even/odd lengths and reusing symmetry.
explanation: Transform string S by inserting boundary characters (e.g. 'abc' -> '#a#b#c#').
Maintain an array P[i] representing the radius of the palindrome centered at i.
Maintain center C and right boundary R of the furthest-reaching palindrome.
For index i:
- Find mirror index i_mirror = 2*C - i.
- If i < R, set initial P[i] = min(R - i, P[i_mirror]).
- Expand around i while characters match.
- If palindrome expands past R, update C = i and R = i + P[i].
Find index with maximum P[i] to extract the longest palindrome.

traceSteps: Step 1: Transform string with delimiters: T = '^#b#a#b#a#d#$'.
Step 2: Maintain center C = 0, right boundary R = 0, radius array P.
Step 3: Expand around centers using mirror i_mirror = 2*C - i.
Max radius found at center 3 (corresponding to 'a' in 'bab'): P[3] = 3.
Step 4: Extract longest palindrome substring from original string -> 'bab'.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds the longest palindromic substring in O(N) time instead of O(N^2) or O(N^3).
wAnswers.whenToUse: When finding longest palindrome or counting palindromic substrings in strict linear time bounds.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Genomic DNA palindromic sequence analysis, text processing, data compression.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Reuses palindrome symmetry (mirroring) to avoid re-expanding characters inside known palindromes.

codeTemplates.code:
def longest_palindrome_manacher(s):
    if not s: return ''
    t = '#' + '#'.join(s) + '#'
    n = len(t)
    p = [0] * n
    c = r = 0
    max_len = max_center = 0

    for i in range(n):
        mirror = 2 * c - i
        if i < r:
            p[i] = min(r - i, p[mirror])
        while i + 1 + p[i] < n and i - 1 - p[i] >= 0 and t[i + 1 + p[i]] == t[i - 1 - p[i]]:
            p[i] += 1
        if i + p[i] > r:
            c = i
            r = i + p[i]
        if p[i] > max_len:
            max_len = p[i]
            max_center = i

    start = (max_center - max_len) // 2
    return s[start : start + max_len]

algorithms.title: Expand Around Center (Palindromic Substrings)
algorithms.summary: Iterates over all 2N-1 potential centers (single characters and gaps between adjacent characters) and expands outward to find all palindromes.
explanation: Every palindrome has a center: single character for odd-length (e.g., 'aba'), or gap for even-length (e.g., 'abba').
For each index i from 0 to N-1:
- Call helper expand(left=i, right=i) for odd length palindromes.
- Call helper expand(left=i, right=i+1) for even length palindromes.
In helper: while left >= 0 and right < N and S[left] == S[right], decrement left and increment right.
Track max length found and return the longest palindrome substring.

traceSteps: Center i=1 ('a'): expand left (0: 'b') & right (2: 'b') -> 'b' == 'b' -> max len = 3 ('bab').
Center i=2 ('b'): expand left (1: 'a') & right (3: 'a') -> 'a' == 'a' -> max len = 3 ('aba').

from collections import Counter

def min_window(s, t):
    if not s or not t: return ''
    target_counts = Counter(t)
    required = len(target_counts)
    window_counts = {}
    formed = 0
    l = r = 0
    ans = (float('inf'), None, None)

    while r < len(s):
        char = s[r]
        window_counts[char] = window_counts.get(char, 0) + 1
        if char in target_counts and window_counts[char] == target_counts[char]:
            formed += 1
        while l <= r and formed == required:
            char = s[l]
            if r - l + 1 < ans[0]:
                ans = (r - l + 1, l, r)
            window_counts[char] -= 1
            if char in target_counts and window_counts[char] < target_counts[char]:
                formed -= 1
            l += 1
        r += 1
    return '' if ans[0] == float('inf') else s[ans[1]:ans[2]+1]

def searchMatrix(matrix: list[list[int]], target: int) -> bool:
    if not matrix or not matrix[0]: return False
    m, n = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])
    low, high = 0, m * n - 1
    
    while low <= high:
        mid = (low + high) // 2
        r, c = mid // n, mid % n
        val = matrix[r][c]
        if val == target: return True
        elif val < target: low = mid + 1
        else: high = mid - 1
    return False

def searchMatrixII(matrix: list[list[int]], target: int) -> bool:
    if not matrix or not matrix[0]: return False
    r, c = 0, len(matrix[0]) - 1
    while r < len(matrix) and c >= 0:
        val = matrix[r][c]
        if val == target: return True
        elif val > target: c -= 1
        else: r += 1
    return False

from collections import Counter

def minWindow(s: str, t: str) -> str:
    if not s or not t: return ""
    target_map = Counter(t)
    required = len(target_map)
    left = 0
    formed = 0
    window_counts = {}
    min_len = float('inf')
    ans_bounds = (0, 0)
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        window_counts[ch] = window_counts.get(ch, 0) + 1
        if ch in target_map and window_counts[ch] == target_map[ch]:
            formed += 1
        while left <= right and formed == required:
            if right - left + 1 < min_len:
                min_len = right - left + 1
                ans_bounds = (left, right)
            l_ch = s[left]
            window_counts[l_ch] -= 1
            if l_ch in target_map and window_counts[l_ch] < target_map[l_ch]:
                formed -= 1
            left += 1
    return "" if min_len == float('inf') else s[ans_bounds[0]:ans_bounds[1]+1]

def checkInclusion(s1: str, s2: str) -> bool:
    if len(s1) > len(s2): return False
    c1, c2 = [0] * 26, [0] * 26
    for i in range(len(s1)):
        c1[ord(s1[i]) - ord('a')] += 1
        c2[ord(s2[i]) - ord('a')] += 1
    if c1 == c2: return True
    for i in range(len(s1), len(s2)):
        c2[ord(s2[i]) - ord('a')] += 1
        c2[ord(s2[i - len(s1)]) - ord('a')] -= 1

algorithms.title: Floyd's Cycle Detection (Tortoise and Hare Algorithm)
algorithms.summary: Detects cycles in a linked list or sequence using two pointers moving at different speeds (slow = 1 step, fast = 2 steps).
explanation: Initialize `slow` and `fast` pointers at head.
Move `slow` by 1 step (`slow = slow.next`) and `fast` by 2 steps (`fast = fast.next.next`).
If there is a cycle, `slow` and `fast` will eventually meet at the same node.
If `fast` reaches `null`, the list has no cycle.
To find cycle entry point: Reset `slow = head`. Move both `slow` and `fast` by 1 step. Their intersection point is the cycle start node.

traceSteps: Phase 1 (Detection): slow moves 1 step, fast moves 2 steps.
Step 3: slow=-4, fast=-4 -> Collision at node -4! Cycle exists.
Phase 2 (Find Entry): Reset slow to head (3), keep fast at collision (-4). Move both 1 step at a time.
Step 1: slow=2, fast=2 -> Met at node 2!
Cycle starting node identified as node 2.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Detects presence of cycles and entry point in linked lists or pseudo-random generator sequences.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When asked if a linked list contains a loop or duplicate number in immutable array range [1, N].
wAnswers.whereUsed: Memory leak detection in circular references, deadlock detection in OS resource graphs, Pollard rho factorization.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Uses zero auxiliary memory O(1) space compared to Hash Set lookup which takes O(N) space.

algorithms.title: Linked List Paradigms: Iterative Pointer Rewiring vs Recursive Top-Down
algorithms.summary: Compares Iterative Pointer Manipulation (Bottom-Up forward traversal O(1) space) against Recursive Stack Rewiring (Top-Down unwinding).
explanation: Iterative Approach (Bottom-Up): Maintain pointers `prev`, `curr`, `next`. Traverse forward in O(1) space, updating `curr.next = prev` step by step.
Recursive Approach (Top-Down): Recurse to the last node first (`new_head = reverse(head.next)`).
During stack unwinding: set `head.next.next = head` and `head.next = None`.
Dummy Node Technique: Initialize `dummy = ListNode(0)` to handle edge cases where head node changes (e.g. deletion, insertion, merging).

traceSteps: Iterative: prev = None, curr = 1. next_node = 2. Set 1.next = None. prev = 1, curr = 2.
Step 2: curr = 2. next_node = 3. Set 2.next = 1. prev = 2, curr = 3.
Step 3: curr = 3. next_node = None. Set 3.next = 2. prev = 3, curr = None.
curr is None -> Loop ends. New head = prev = 3.
Recursive unwinding: Recurse 1->2->3. Base case at 3 returns head 3. Unwind at 2: 2.next.next=2 (3->2). Unwind at 1: 1.next.next=1 (2->1).
Both paradigms result in reversed list: 3 -> 2 -> 1 -> None.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Mastery of pointer manipulation and recursive stack unwinding in sequential nodes.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Iterative for O(1) memory efficiency; Recursive for clean subproblem formulation.
wAnswers.whereUsed: LRU Cache doubly linked lists, OS kernel thread list scheduling, undo history buffers.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: O(N) linear time pass over all nodes.

codeTemplates.code:
# Iterative O(1) Space
def reverse_iterative(head):
    prev, curr = None, head
    while curr:
        nxt = curr.next
        curr.next = prev
        prev = curr
        curr = nxt
    return prev

# Recursive Top-Down
def reverse_recursive(head):
    if not head or not head.next:
        return head
    new_head = reverse_recursive(head.next)
    head.next.next = head
    head.next = None
    return new_head

algorithms.title: Merge Two Sorted Linked Lists (Iterative & Recursive)
algorithms.summary: Combines two sorted linked lists into a single sorted list by updating pointers in O(M+N) time.
explanation: Dummy Node Pattern: Create `dummy = ListNode(-1)` and `tail = dummy`.
Compare `l1.val` and `l2.val`.
If `l1.val <= l2.val`: attach `tail.next = l1` and advance `l1 = l1.next`.
Else: attach `tail.next = l2` and advance `l2 = l2.next`.
Advance `tail = tail.next`.
Attach remaining non-empty list (`tail.next = l1 if l1 else l2`) and return `dummy.next`.

traceSteps: Compare 1 vs 1: attach l1 (1), l1 moves to 2. List = -1 -> 1.
Compare 2 vs 1: attach l2 (1), l2 moves to 3. List = -1 -> 1 -> 1.
Compare 2 vs 3: attach l1 (2), l1 moves to 4. List = -1 -> 1 -> 1 -> 2.
Compare 4 vs 3: attach l2 (3), l2 moves to 4. List = -1 -> 1 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3.
Compare 4 vs 4: attach l1 (4), l1 moves to None.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Combines 2 sorted linked sequences without instantiating new node memory.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When performing Merge Sort on linked lists or merging sorted data streams.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Merge Sort for linked lists, database external sort-merge join step.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: O(M + N) time with zero extra node memory allocated.

algorithms.title: Fast & Slow Pointer Pattern (Middle Finding & Cycle)
algorithms.summary: Uses two pointers moving at different speeds (slow by 1, fast by 2) to find the middle node or detect cycles in single pass.
explanation: Initialize `slow = head` and `fast = head`.
While `fast` is not None and `fast.next` is not None:
- Advance `slow = slow.next` (1 step).
- Advance `fast = fast.next.next` (2 steps).
When `fast` reaches the end, `slow` will be exactly at the middle node of the list!
For even-length lists: `slow` rests at second middle node.

traceSteps: Step 3: fast.next is None -> Loop terminates.
Middle Node = 3 found in a single pass O(N) time & O(1) space.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Locates the middle of a linked list or detects cycles in single-pass O(1) space.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When splitting a linked list into two equal halves (e.g. Merge Sort, Palindrome check).
wAnswers.whereUsed: Linked list merge sort partition, palindrome verification, cycle start detection.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: O(N) single-pass with zero extra space.

algorithms.title: Remove N-th Node From End of List (Two-Pointer Gap)
algorithms.summary: Removes the N-th node from the end of a linked list in a single pass using a dummy node and a fixed-gap two-pointer technique.
explanation: Initialize `dummy` node pointing to `head` (handles head deletion edge case).
Set `first = dummy` and `second = dummy`.
Advance `first` pointer by `n + 1` steps to create a fixed gap of size `n` between `first` and `second`.
Move both `first` and `second` forward together until `first` reaches `None`.
Now `second` points to the node BEFORE the target node!
Perform deletion: `second.next = second.next.next` and return `dummy.next`.

traceSteps: Advance first by n+1 (3 steps): first = node 3.
first is None -> second rests at node 3 (node before 4).

algorithms.title: Merge Sort on Linked List (Top-Down Divide & Conquer O(N log N))
algorithms.summary: Sorts a linked list in O(N log N) time by finding the middle, splitting into two halves, recursively sorting both, and merging.
explanation: Base Case: If `head` is None or `head.next` is None, return `head`.
Divide: Find middle node using Fast & Slow pointers. Split list into `left` half and `right` half (`mid.next = None`).
Conquer: Recursively call `sortList(left)` and `sortList(right)`.
Combine: Merge the two sorted halves using `mergeTwoLists(left, right)` and return merged head.

Recursively sort right [1, 3]: split to [1] and [3] -> Merge returns [1, 3].

algorithms.title: Singly Linked List Foundations & Operations
algorithms.summary: Linear node structure where each node holds data and a single forward pointer ('next') to the succeeding node.
explanation: A Singly Linked List consists of dynamically allocated nodes connected sequentially via 'next' pointers.
Head pointer stores the start of the list. Last node points to None/null.
Insertion/Deletion at Head takes O(1) time. Searching or accessing by index K takes O(K) time.
Reversing a Singly Linked List requires updating 'next' pointers in a single pass using prev, curr, and nxt pointers.

traceSteps: Reverse List: Iterate updating pointers: prev=None, curr=30.
Final Head points to 10: Head -> [10] -> [20] -> [30] -> None

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Provides dynamic size allocation without requiring contiguous physical memory allocation.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When frequent insertions and deletions at the head are needed without array resizing penalties.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Stack data structure implementation, hash table chaining for collision resolution, OS memory allocation blocks.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Avoids O(N) array element shifts during insertions and deletions.

algorithms.title: Doubly Linked List Foundations & Operations
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(1) Insertion & Deletion with direct node reference
algorithms.summary: Bi-directional node structure where each node holds data, a forward pointer ('next'), and a backward pointer ('prev').
explanation: A Doubly Linked List allows two-way traversal (forward and backward).
Each node has both `prev` and `next` pointers. Head's `prev` is None, and Tail's `next` is None.
Deletion of a specific node given its pointer takes O(1) time because `node.prev.next = node.next` and `node.next.prev = node.prev` directly access neighbors.
Reversing a Doubly Linked List is simplified by swapping `prev` and `next` pointers for every node.

wAnswers.whenToUse: When backward traversal or fast removal of nodes from middle/tail is required.
wAnswers.whereUsed: LRU Cache (HashMap + Doubly Linked List), Browser history back/forward navigation, Music player queues.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Provides constant time O(1) removal of any node given its reference.

algorithms.title: Circular Singly Linked List
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(1) Insert at Head/Tail with Tail pointer, O(N) Traversal
algorithms.summary: Singly Linked List variant where the last node ('tail') points back to the first node ('head'), forming a closed loop.
explanation: In a Circular Singly Linked List, there is no Null termination. The last node's `next` pointer links back to `head`.
Maintaining a `tail` pointer allows O(1) insertions at both head (`tail.next`) and tail.
Traversal loops continuously until `curr == head` again.
Useful for round-robin scheduling algorithms where process loops continuously.

algorithms.title: Circular Doubly Linked List
algorithms.summary: Doubly Linked List variant where Head's `prev` points to Tail, and Tail's `next` points to Head, enabling instantaneous bidirectional loop navigation.
explanation: Combines advantages of Doubly Linked List and Circular Linked List.
`head.prev` directly gives `tail`, and `tail.next` directly gives `head` in O(1) time without keeping a separate tail variable.
Node insertion and deletion at both ends involve updating 4 pointer references (`prev` & `next` for adjacent nodes).
Extremely powerful structure for deque implementations and Fibonacci Heaps.

algorithms.title: Merge K Sorted Linked Lists
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(N log K) where N is total nodes, K is number of lists
algorithms.summary: Merges K sorted linked lists into a single sorted linked list using a Min-Heap or Divide & Conquer approach.
explanation: Push the head node of all K lists into a Min-Heap Priority Queue.
Repeatedly pop the smallest node from the heap, attach it to the merged list, and push its `next` node into the heap.
Alternatively, merge lists pairwise using Divide & Conquer (merge 2 lists at a time).
Achieves optimal O(N log K) time complexity.

traceSteps: Push initial heads (1 from L1, 1 from L2, 2 from L3) into Min-Heap.

wAnswers.whenToUse: When merging multiple sorted logs, database partitions, or sorted linked list chains.

algorithms.title: Intersection of Two Linked Lists
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(N + M) where N, M are lengths of the two lists
algorithms.summary: Finds the node at which two singly linked lists intersect using two pointer traversal.
explanation: Initialize pointer `pA` at headA and pointer `pB` at headB.
Traverse both lists. When `pA` reaches the end of list A, redirect it to headB.
When `pB` reaches the end of list B, redirect it to headA.
If the lists intersect, `pA` and `pB` will meet at the intersection node after traversing (LenA + LenB) steps.
If no intersection exists, both pointers will equal Null simultaneously.

exampleTrace.input: List A: [4, 1, 8, 4, 5], List B: [5, 6, 1, 8, 4, 5], Intersect at node 8
traceSteps: Advance both pointers. pA reaches end of A first, redirects to 5 (headB).
pB reaches end of B, redirects to 4 (headA).
Both pointers are now synchronized in distance to the intersection point!
pA and pB advance simultaneously and meet at node 8. Return node 8.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds the exact memory junction node shared by two merging linked list paths.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When detecting shared memory nodes or merged execution graphs without modifying data.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Garbage collector reference counts, git commit branch merge base identification.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Requires zero extra space O(1) and exact single pass O(N+M).

codeTemplates.code:
def getIntersectionNode(headA: ListNode, headB: ListNode) -> ListNode:
    if not headA or not headB: return None
    pA, pB = headA, headB
    while pA != pB:
        pA = pA.next if pA else headB
        pB = pB.next if pB else headA
    return pA

algorithms.title: Flatten a Multilevel Linked List
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(N) where N is total nodes across all levels
algorithms.spaceComplexity: O(N) for recursion stack or O(1) iterative pointer modification
algorithms.summary: Flattens a 2D or multilevel linked list with `child` pointers into a single-level doubly/singly linked list.
explanation: Iterate through nodes. When a node has a `child` pointer:
Find the tail node of the child list.
Connect child tail's `next` pointer to `curr.next`.
Connect `curr.next` to `curr.child` and set `curr.child = None`.
Continue iterating until all levels are flattened into 1D.

traceSteps: Iterate curr to Node 3. Detect child Node 7.
Find tail of child list: Node 8.
Connect Node 3.next to Node 7 and clear child pointer.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Transforms hierarchical 2D node graphs into a linear sequence.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When unnesting recursive linked structures into a single continuous stream.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Document tree flattening, DOM element sequence linearization, compiler AST unrolling.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Linear O(N) traversal without duplicating node data.

codeTemplates.code:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, val, prev=None, next=None, child=None):
        self.val = val
        self.prev = prev
        self.next = next
        self.child = child

def flatten(head: 'Node') -> 'Node':
    if not head: return None
    curr = head
    while curr:
        if curr.child:
            nxt = curr.next
            child_tail = curr.child
            while child_tail.next:
                child_tail = child_tail.next
            child_tail.next = nxt
            if nxt: nxt.prev = child_tail
            curr.next = curr.child
            curr.child.prev = curr
            curr.child = None
        curr = curr.next
    return head

algorithms.title: Clone Linked List with Random Pointer
algorithms.spaceComplexity: O(1) extra space using node interleaving (or O(N) using HashMap)
algorithms.summary: Creates a deep copy of a linked list where each node contains an extra `random` pointer referencing any node or Null.
explanation: Method (Interleaving):
Step 1: Create copied node A' right after original node A (A -> A' -> B -> B').
Step 2: Assign random pointers: `curr.next.random = curr.random.next` if `curr.random` exists.
Step 3: Separate original list and cloned list by updating `next` pointers.
Returns head of deep cloned list in O(N) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

traceSteps: Step 3 (Separate): Extract [7', 13'] into independent cloned list.

wAnswers.whenToUse: When cloning memory structures with arbitrary pointers without modifying originals.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Object graph serialization, deep copy state cloning, virtual machine heap duplication.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Interleaving nodes avoids O(N) extra hash map memory overhead.

codeTemplates.code:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, x: int, next: 'Node' = None, random: 'Node' = None):
        self.val = int(x)
        self.next = next
        self.random = random

def copyRandomList(head: 'Node') -> 'Node':
    if not head: return None
    
    # Step 1: Interleave cloned nodes
    curr = head
    while curr:
        nxt = curr.next
        copy = Node(curr.val, nxt)
        curr.next = copy
        curr = nxt
        
    # Step 2: Assign random pointers
    curr = head
    while curr:
        if curr.random:
            curr.next.random = curr.random.next
        curr = curr.next.next
        
    # Step 3: Separate lists
    curr = head
    dummy = Node(0)
    copy_curr = dummy
    while curr:
        nxt = curr.next.next
        copy = curr.next
        copy_curr.next = copy
        copy_curr = copy
        curr.next = nxt
        curr = nxt
        
    return dummy.next

algorithms.title: Palindrome Linked List
algorithms.summary: Checks if a singly linked list is a palindrome in O(N) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
explanation: Step 1: Find the middle of the linked list using Fast & Slow pointers.
Step 2: Reverse the second half of the linked list in-place.
Step 3: Compare values of the first half and reversed second half node-by-node.
Step 4: (Optional) Restore the original list structure by re-reversing the second half.
Returns True if symmetric, False otherwise.

traceSteps: Find middle using fast/slow pointer: slow points to 2nd '2'.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Determines whether node values form a palindrome without extra array memory.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When checking symmetry in linked structures with strict O(1) space constraint.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Bioinformatics DNA sequence symmetry checks, text processing queues.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Reversing second half in-place achieves linear O(N) time with zero extra space O(1).

codeTemplates.code:
def isPalindrome(head: ListNode) -> bool:
    if not head or not head.next: return True
    
    # Step 1: Find middle
    slow, fast = head, head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
        
    # Step 2: Reverse second half
    prev = None
    curr = slow
    while curr:
        nxt = curr.next
        curr.next = prev
        prev = curr
        curr = nxt
        
    # Step 3: Compare halves
    first, second = head, prev
    while second:
        if first.val != second.val:
            return False
        first = first.next
        second = second.next
        
    return True

algorithms.title: Sort Linked List (Merge Sort O(N log N))
algorithms.spaceComplexity: O(log N) recursion stack space (or O(1) iterative bottom-up)
algorithms.summary: Sorts a linked list in O(N log N) time using Top-Down or Bottom-Up Merge Sort.
explanation: Split list into two halves using Fast & Slow pointer middle finding.
Recursively sort left and right sublists.
Merge two sorted sublists together using standard two-pointer merge algorithm.
Optimal sorting algorithm for linked list memory structures.

traceSteps: Split list at middle: Left [4, 2], Right [1, 3].
Merge [2, 4] and [1, 3]: Compare 2 & 1 -> append 1. Compare 2 & 3 -> append 2. Compare 4 & 3 -> append 3. Append remaining 4.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Sorts linked list nodes efficiently without converting to array.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When sorting linked lists in guaranteed O(N log N) time.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Sorting external dynamic memory lists, kernel task priority sorting.

codeTemplates.code:
def sortList(head: ListNode) -> ListNode:
    if not head or not head.next: return head
    
    # Find middle (slow will point to node before mid)
    slow, fast = head, head.next
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
        
    mid = slow.next
    slow.next = None  # Cut list
    
    left = sortList(head)
    right = sortList(mid)
    
    # Merge sorted lists
    dummy = ListNode(0)
    curr = dummy
    while left and right:
        if left.val < right.val:
            curr.next = left
            left = left.next
        else:
            curr.next = right
            right = right.next
        curr = curr.next
    curr.next = left or right
    return dummy.next

algorithms.title: Next Greater Element I & II (NGE)
algorithms.summary: Find the first element to the right that is strictly greater than the current element (Linear & Circular Array).
explanation: Monotonic Decreasing Stack Strategy: Maintain a stack storing element values/indices in strictly decreasing order.
Algorithm for Linear Array: Traverse array right-to-left (or left-to-right).
1) While stack is not empty and `stack.top() <= curr_val`: Pop element from stack.
2) If stack is empty: NGE is `-1`. Else: NGE is `stack.top()`.
3) Push `curr_val` onto stack.
Circular Array Variant (NGE II): Simulate 2N iterations using index `i % N` so elements can wrap around to find next greater.

traceSteps: Step 1: Traverse right-to-left starting at 8. Stack = []. NGE[8] = -1. Push 8. Stack=[8].
Step 2: Element 10. Pop 8 (10 >= 8). Stack empty. NGE[10] = -1. Push 10. Stack=[10].
Step 3: Element 2. Stack top (10) > 2. NGE[2] = 10. Push 2. Stack=[10, 2].
Step 4: Element 5. Pop 2 (5 >= 2). Stack top (10) > 5. NGE[5] = 10. Push 5. Stack=[10, 5].
Step 5: Element 4. Stack top (5) > 4. NGE[4] = 5. Push 4. Stack=[10, 5, 4].

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds nearest greater element to the right in linear O(N) single pass.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When finding next larger value or nearest right-side peak boundary.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Stock span calculation, temperature rise forecasting, histogram bounds.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Each element is pushed and popped at most once, yielding O(N) time.

algorithms.title: Next Smaller Element (NSE)
algorithms.summary: Find the first element to the right that is strictly smaller than the current element.
explanation: Monotonic Increasing Stack Strategy: Maintain a stack storing elements in strictly increasing order.
Traverse array right-to-left:
1) While stack is not empty and `stack.top() >= curr_val`: Pop element from stack.
2) If stack is empty: NSE is `-1`. Else: NSE is `stack.top()`.
3) Push `curr_val` onto stack.

traceSteps: Step 2: i=3 (val 2): Pop 25 (25 >= 2). Stack empty. NSE = -1. Push 2.
Step 3: i=2 (val 5): Stack top 2 < 5. NSE = 2. Push 5.
Step 4: i=1 (val 8): Stack top 5 < 8. NSE = 5. Push 8.
Step 5: i=0 (val 4): Pop 8 and 5 (>= 4). Stack top 2 < 4. NSE = 2.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds nearest smaller element to the right in O(N) time.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When determining right boundary for histogram rectangles.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Histogram area computation, minimum range boundaries.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: O(N) linear time Monotonic Stack.

algorithms.title: Previous Smaller Element (PSE)
algorithms.summary: Find the first element to the left that is strictly smaller than the current element.
explanation: Monotonic Increasing Stack (Left-to-Right Pass):
Traverse array left-to-right:
1) While stack is not empty and `stack.top() >= curr_val`: Pop element from stack.
2) If stack is empty: PSE is `-1`. Else: PSE is `stack.top()`.
3) Push `curr_val` onto stack.

traceSteps: Step 2: i=1 (val 5): Stack top 4 < 5. PSE = 4. Push 5.
Step 3: i=2 (val 2): Pop 5 and 4 (>= 2). Stack empty. PSE = -1. Push 2.
Step 4: i=3 (val 10): Stack top 2 < 10. PSE = 2. Push 10.
Step 5: i=4 (val 8): Pop 10 (>= 8). Stack top 2 < 8. PSE = 2. Push 8.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds nearest smaller element to the left in O(N) single pass.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When determining left boundary for histogram bar expansion.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Largest Rectangle in Histogram, stock span calculation.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: O(N) linear time Monotonic Stack.

algorithms.title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
algorithms.summary: Find area of largest rectangle that can be formed within a histogram of bar heights using Monotonic Stack boundaries.
explanation: Histogram Boundary Formula: For each bar at index `i` with height `h = heights[i]`, the max rectangular width it can span is `width = right_bound - left_bound - 1`.
`left_bound` = index of Previous Smaller Element (PSE).

def largestRectangleArea(heights: list[int]) -> int:
    stack = [] # Stores indices
    max_area = 0
    heights.append(0) # Sentinel
    for i, h in enumerate(heights):
        while stack and heights[stack[-1]] > h:
            height = heights[stack.pop()]
            width = i if not stack else (i - stack[-1] - 1)
            max_area = max(max_area, height * width)
        stack.append(i)
    heights.pop()
    return max_area

algorithms.title: Sliding Window Maximum (Monotonic Deque)
algorithms.summary: Find the maximum element in every sliding window of size K as it moves from left to right across array.
explanation: Monotonic Decreasing Deque Strategy: Maintain a Double-Ended Queue (Deque) storing array indices such that corresponding values `nums[idx]` are in strictly decreasing order.
Algorithm for each index `i`:
1) Out of Window Eviction: If `deque.front() <= i - K`, pop front of deque.
2) Monotonic Maintenance: While deque is not empty and `nums[deque.back()] <= nums[i]`, pop back of deque.
3) Push `i` to back of deque.
4) When `i >= K - 1`, record window maximum `nums[deque.front()]`.

traceSteps: Step 3: i=2 (val -1): Deque = [1, 2]. Window 1 result: nums[1] = 3.
Step 4: i=3 (val -3): Deque = [1, 2, 3]. Window 2 result: nums[1] = 3.
Step 5: i=4 (val 5): Pop out of window 1. Pop 2, 3 (<= 5). Deque = [4]. Window 3 result: nums[4] = 5.
Step 6: Continue for all windows -> Output = [3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7].

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Computes rolling maximum in sliding window of size K in O(N) total time.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When finding maximum or minimum in fixed sliding time windows.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Real-time stock price peak monitor, network packet latency max burst filter.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Deque elements are pushed/popped at most once, reducing O(N*K) naive loop to O(N).

algorithms.title: Trapping Rain Water (Monotonic Stack & Two Pointers)
algorithms.summary: Calculate total trapped rainwater between elevation bars using Two Pointers or Monotonic Stack boundaries.
explanation: Water Trapping Condition: Water trapped at index `i` is `min(left_max, right_max) - height[i]`.
Two Pointers Strategy (O(1) Space): Maintain `left` and `right` pointers, along with `left_max` and `right_max`.
If `height[left] <= height[right]`: If `height[left] >= left_max`, update `left_max`; else add `left_max - height[left]` to total water. Move `left++`.
Else (`height[left] > height[right]`): If `height[right] >= right_max`, update `right_max`; else add `right_max - height[right]` to total water. Move `right--`.

Step 2: Trapped water accumulates at indices 2 (1 unit), 4 (1 unit), 5 (2 units), 6 (1 unit), 9 (1 unit).

wAnswers.whenToUse: When computing volume of trapped liquid or bounded valley capacity.

codeTemplates.code:
def trap(height: list[int]) -> int:
    if not height: return 0
    l, r = 0, len(height) - 1
    left_max, right_max = height[l], height[r]
    water = 0
    while l < r:
        if left_max <= right_max:
            l += 1
            left_max = max(left_max, height[l])
            water += left_max - height[l]
        else:
            r -= 1
            right_max = max(right_max, height[r])
            water += right_max - height[r]
    return water

def inorderTraversal(root: TreeNode) -> list[int]:
    res, stack = [], []
    curr = root
    while curr or stack:
        while curr:
            stack.append(curr)
            curr = curr.left
        curr = stack.pop()
        res.append(curr.val)
        curr = curr.right
    return res

from collections import defaultdict, deque

def verticalTraversal(root: TreeNode) -> list[list[int]]:
    nodes = defaultdict(list)
    queue = deque([(root, 0, 0)])
    while queue:
        node, col, row = queue.popleft()
        if node:
            nodes[col].append((row, node.val))
            queue.append((node.left, col - 1, row + 1))
            queue.append((node.right, col + 1, row + 1))
            
    res = []
    for c in sorted(nodes.keys()):
        col_nodes = sorted(nodes[c], key=lambda x: (x[0], x[1]))
        res.append([val for r, val in col_nodes])
    return res

algorithms.title: Morris Traversal (Inorder & Preorder in O(1) Auxiliary Space)
algorithms.summary: Traverse binary tree in Inorder/Preorder sequence without recursion or stack using Threaded Binary Tree pointers (`pred.right = curr`).
explanation: Threaded Binary Tree Concept: Utilize null right pointers of leaf nodes to point back to their inorder predecessor parent.
Algorithm Steps: 1) If `curr.left` is null, process `curr.val` and move `curr = curr.right`.
2) Otherwise, find `curr`'s Inorder Predecessor (`pred = curr.left` while `pred.right and pred.right != curr`).
3) If `pred.right` is null, set `pred.right = curr` (create thread) and move `curr = curr.left`.
4) If `pred.right == curr`, revert thread `pred.right = None`, process `curr.val`, and move `curr = curr.right`.

Step 4: At node 2. Find predecessor -> Node 1. `pred.right == 2` (thread exists). Break thread `1.right = None`. Process 2 -> [1, 2]. Move to right child 3.
Step 5: At node 3. Left child is null. Process 3 -> [1, 2, 3]. Right child is null.
Step 6: Traversal Complete. Tree structure fully restored!

2) Recurse left and right: `left = LCA(root.left, p, q)`, `right = LCA(root.right, p, q)`.
3) Decision: If BOTH `left` and `right` are non-null, `root` is the LCA! Return `root`.
4) If only one is non-null, return the non-null child.

algorithms.title: Maximum Path Sum in Binary Tree
algorithms.summary: Find maximum path sum where path can start and end at any node in binary tree.
explanation: Path Definition: Sequence of nodes connected by parent-child edges where no node appears more than once.
Bottom-Up Postorder helper function `max_gain(node)`.
Left gain = `max(0, max_gain(node.left))`, Right gain = `max(0, max_gain(node.right))`.
Path turning at node = `node.val + left_gain + right_gain`. Update global `max_sum = max(max_sum, path_turning)`.
Return `node.val + max(left_gain, right_gain)` up to parent.

Step 4: Node 20 returns gain to parent: 20 + max(15, 7) = 35.
Step 6: Global Maximum Path Sum remains 42.

codeTemplates.code:
def maxPathSum(root: TreeNode) -> int:
    max_sum = float('-inf')
    def max_gain(node):
        nonlocal max_sum
        if not node: return 0
        left_gain = max(0, max_gain(node.left))
        right_gain = max(0, max_gain(node.right))
        current_path = node.val + left_gain + right_gain
        max_sum = max(max_sum, current_path)
        return node.val + max(left_gain, right_gain)
    max_gain(root)
    return max_sum

def diameterOfBinaryTree(root: TreeNode) -> int:
    diameter = 0
    def height(node):
        nonlocal diameter
        if not node: return 0
        lh = height(node.left)
        rh = height(node.right)
        diameter = max(diameter, lh + rh)
        return 1 + max(lh, rh)
    height(root)
    return diameter

def isSymmetric(root: TreeNode) -> bool:
    def isMirror(t1, t2):
        if not t1 and not t2: return True
        if not t1 or not t2: return False
        return (t1.val == t2.val and 
                isMirror(t1.left, t2.right) and 
                isMirror(t1.right, t2.left))
    return isMirror(root.left, root.right) if root else True

def invertTree(root: TreeNode) -> TreeNode:

    root.left, root.right = root.right, root.left
    invertTree(root.left)
    invertTree(root.right)

algorithms.title: Binary Tree Path Sums (Path Sum I, II & III)
algorithms.summary: Master Path Sum problems: Root-to-Leaf target sum verification (Path Sum I), collecting all Root-to-Leaf path sequences (Path Sum II), and Prefix Sum HashMap for arbitrary downward paths (Path Sum III).
explanation: Path Sum I: Top-down recursion `hasPathSum(node, remainingSum - node.val)`. True if leaf node has `remainingSum == node.val`.
Path Sum II: Collect paths in `current_path` list. Backtrack `current_path.pop()` after recursing.

Path Sum III (Arbitrary Downward Paths): Use Prefix Sum HashMap `prefix_map[curr_sum]`. At node, `curr_sum += node.val`. Target paths ending at node = `prefix_map[curr_sum - targetSum]`. Update map, recurse children, then remove `curr_sum` from map (backtrack).

# Path Sum I
def hasPathSum(root: TreeNode, targetSum: int) -> bool:
    if not root: return False
    if not root.left and not root.right:
        return root.val == targetSum
    return (hasPathSum(root.left, targetSum - root.val) or 
            hasPathSum(root.right, targetSum - root.val))

# Path Sum III (Prefix Sum HashMap)
from collections import defaultdict
def pathSum3(root: TreeNode, targetSum: int) -> int:
    prefix = defaultdict(int)
    prefix[0] = 1
    def dfs(node, curr_sum):
        if not node: return 0
        curr_sum += node.val
        count = prefix[curr_sum - targetSum]
        prefix[curr_sum] += 1
        count += dfs(node.left, curr_sum) + dfs(node.right, curr_sum)
        prefix[curr_sum] -= 1 # Backtrack
        return count
    return dfs(root, 0)

algorithms.title: Count Nodes in Complete Binary Tree in O(log^2 N)
algorithms.summary: Count total nodes in a Complete Binary Tree in O(log^2 N) time by exploiting complete tree height matching properties.
explanation: Complete Binary Tree Property: All levels except possibly the last are completely filled, and all nodes in the last level are as far left as possible.
Algorithm: Compare Left Height `left_h` (traverse left child chain) and Right Height `right_h` (traverse right child chain).
1) If `left_h == right_h`: The subtree is a Perfect Binary Tree! Total nodes = `2^left_h - 1` (computed via bit shift `(1 << left_h) - 1`).
2) If `left_h != right_h`: Recurse `1 + countNodes(node.left) + countNodes(node.right)`.

Step 2: Recurse left on node 2: left_h = 2, right_h = 2 (equal!). Total nodes at node 2 = (1 << 2) - 1 = 3 nodes.
Step 3: Recurse right on node 3: left_h = 2, right_h = 1 (not equal). Subtree has 2 nodes.

def deleteNode(root, key):
    if not root: return None
    if key < root.val:
        root.left = deleteNode(root.left, key)
    elif key > root.val:
        root.right = deleteNode(root.right, key)
    else:
        if not root.left: return root.right
        if not root.right: return root.left
        curr = root.right
        while curr.left: curr = curr.left
        root.val = curr.val
        root.right = deleteNode(root.right, curr.val)
    return root

def getAllElements(root1, root2) -> list[int]:
    def inorder(node, lst):
        if not node: return
        inorder(node.left, lst)
        lst.append(node.val)
        inorder(node.right, lst)
    l1, l2 = [], []
    inorder(root1, l1)
    inorder(root2, l2)
    i = j = 0
    res = []
    while i < len(l1) and j < len(l2):
        if l1[i] < l2[j]:
            res.append(l1[i]); i += 1
        else:
            res.append(l2[j]); j += 1
    res.extend(l1[i:])
    res.extend(l2[j:])
    return res

def findTarget(root, k: int) -> bool:
    def push_left(node, st):
        while node: st.append(node); node = node.left
    def push_right(node, st):
        while node: st.append(node); node = node.right
    st_left, st_right = [], []

    push_right(root, st_right)

    right_node = st_right[-1]

        v1, v2 = left_node.val, right_node.val
        if v1 + v2 == k: return True
        if v1 + v2 < k:
            node = st_left.pop()
            push_left(node.right, st_left)
            left_node = st_left[-1] if st_left else None
        else:
            node = st_right.pop()
            push_right(node.left, st_right)
            right_node = st_right[-1] if st_right else None
    return False

algorithms.title: Dijkstra's Algorithm (Shortest Path in Weighted Graph)
algorithms.summary: Finds the shortest distance from a single source node to all other nodes in a non-negatively weighted graph using a Min-Heap.
explanation: Maintain a `dist` array initialized to infinity, with `dist[source] = 0`.
Use a Min-Heap (Priority Queue) to store `(current_distance, node)`.
Pop the node with smallest distance `u` from heap.
For each neighbor `v` of `u` with edge weight `w`:
- If `dist[u] + w < dist[v]`, update `dist[v] = dist[u] + w` and push `(dist[v], v)` into heap.
Repeat until min-heap is empty.

traceSteps: Initialize dist = [0, inf, inf, inf], min-heap = [(0, 0)].
Pop (0, 0): Relax neighbor 1 (dist[1] = min(inf, 0+4) = 4), relax neighbor 2 (dist[2] = min(inf, 0+2) = 2). Heap = [(2, 2), (4, 1)].
Pop (2, 2): Relax neighbor 1 via 2 (dist[1] = min(4, 2+1) = 3). Heap = [(3, 1), (4, 1)].

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Calculates minimum cost or distance path from source node to all other nodes in non-negative weighted graphs.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When given a weighted graph (no negative weights) and asked for shortest path or min cost traversal.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Google Maps GPS navigation routing, OSPF internet routing protocol, game pathfinding (A* basis).
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Min-Heap prioritization guarantees we process nodes in increasing distance order, ensuring O((V + E) log V) efficiency.

algorithms.title: Topological Sort & Kahn's Algorithm (DAG Scheduling)
algorithms.summary: Produces a linear ordering of vertices in a Directed Acyclic Graph where every directed edge u→v places u before v.
explanation: Compute `in-degree` (number of incoming edges) for every vertex.
Push all vertices with `in-degree == 0` into a Queue.
While Queue is not empty:
- Pop node `u`, add it to topological result list.
- For each neighbor `v` of `u`, decrement `in-degree[v]--`.
- If `in-degree[v] == 0`, push `v` into Queue.
If result list length equals V, DAG is valid. Otherwise, a cycle exists!

traceSteps: Push inDegree==0 nodes into Queue: Queue = [3].
Pop 3: Add to topo order [3]. Decrement inDegrees of neighbors 1 & 2 -> inDegree[1]=0, inDegree[2]=0. Queue = [1, 2].
Pop 1: Add to topo order [3, 1]. Decrement neighbor 0 -> inDegree[0] = 1. Queue = [2].
Pop 2: Add to topo order [3, 1, 2]. Decrement neighbor 0 -> inDegree[0] = 0. Queue = [0].
Pop 0: Add to topo order [3, 1, 2, 0]. Queue empty.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Determines a valid task execution order when tasks have prerequisites or dependencies.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When given prerequisites (Course Schedule), build tool dependencies (npm/cmake), or cycle detection in directed graph.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Build systems (Webpack/Bazel dependency resolution), course prerequisite planning, Airflow DAG task scheduler.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Linear O(V + E) processing time using in-degree BFS queue.

from collections import deque

def findOrder(numCourses, prerequisites):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(numCourses)]
    indegree = [0] * numCourses
    for dest, src in prerequisites:
        adj[src].append(dest)
        indegree[dest] += 1
        
    queue = deque([i for i in range(numCourses) if indegree[i] == 0])
    topo_order = []
    
    while queue:
        u = queue.popleft()
        topo_order.append(u)
        for v in adj[u]:
            indegree[v] -= 1
            if indegree[v] == 0:
                queue.append(v)
                
    return topo_order if len(topo_order) == numCourses else []

algorithms.title: Disjoint Set Union (DSU / Union-Find with Rank & Path Compression)
algorithms.summary: Tracks partitioned sets and connects elements in near-constant O(α(N)) time using Path Compression and Union by Rank.
explanation: Maintain `parent` array where `parent[i] = i` initially, and `rank` array initialized to 0.
`find(i)`: Recursively find root of `i`. Apply Path Compression (`parent[i] = find(parent[i])`) to flatten tree.
`union(i, j)`: Find roots `rootI` and `rootJ`. If different, attach smaller rank tree under larger rank tree.
Inverse Ackermann function α(N) is effectively <= 4 for all realistic values of N, making ops practically O(1)!

Union(2, 3): Find(2) -> path compress parent[2]=1 -> root 1. Find(3) = 3. Make parent[3] = 1, rank[1] = 2. Parent = [0, 1, 1, 1].
Connected(1, 3): Find(1) = 1, Find(3) = 1. Ultimate roots match (1 == 1)!
Returns True in O(alpha(N)) nearly constant time.

algorithms.title: Breadth-First Search (BFS) & Unweighted Shortest Path
algorithms.summary: Explores a graph level-by-level starting from a source vertex using a FIFO Queue. Guarantees the shortest path in unweighted graphs.
explanation: Initialize a `visited` set / boolean array and a FIFO `Queue`.
Push source vertex `start` into Queue and mark `visited[start] = True`.
While Queue is not empty: pop front vertex `u`.
For each unvisited neighbor `v` of `u`: set `dist[v] = dist[u] + 1`, mark `visited[v] = True`, and enqueue `v`.
Repeat level order exploration until queue becomes empty.

traceSteps: Pop 0: Process neighbors of 0 -> 1 and 2. Enqueue 1 and 2. Queue = [1, 2], visited = {0, 1, 2}, dist = {1:1, 2:1}.
Pop 1: Process neighbor of 1 -> 3. Enqueue 3. Queue = [2, 3], visited = {0, 1, 2, 3}, dist = {3:2}.
Pop 2: Process neighbor of 2 -> 4. Enqueue 4. Queue = [3, 4], visited = {0, 1, 2, 3, 4}, dist = {4:2}.
Pop 4: No unvisited neighbors. Queue empty.
BFS Order = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]. Shortest path lengths computed in O(V + E).

Iterate through all unvisited neighbors `v` of `u`.
Recursively call DFS on each unvisited neighbor `v`.

algorithms.summary: Detects if an undirected graph contains a cycle by tracking the parent of each visited vertex during traversal.
explanation: Perform BFS/DFS from each unvisited vertex.
Keep track of `(node, parent)` during traversal.
If an adjacent node `v` is already visited AND `v != parent`, a cycle exists!
Return True immediately upon detecting an already-visited non-parent neighbor.

Check neighbors of 2: neighbor 0 is visited, and 0 != parent (1)!
Since neighbor 0 is already visited and is not parent, cycle (0-1-2-0) is detected!

algorithms.title: Cycle Detection in Directed Graph (Recursion Stack & Kahn)
algorithms.summary: Detects cycles in directed graphs using active recursion stack tracking or Kahn's topological count check.
explanation: Maintain two state arrays: `visited` and `inStack` (path array).
When entering a vertex `u`, mark `visited[u] = True` and `inStack[u] = True`.
For neighbor `v`: if `inStack[v] == True`, a back-edge exists $\rightarrow$ Cycle detected!
When exiting recursion for `u`, reset `inStack[u] = False`.
Alternatively using Kahn's algo: If topo sort processed count < Total vertices V, a cycle exists.

algorithms.title: Bipartite Graph Check (Two-Coloring Algorithm)
algorithms.summary: Determines whether vertices can be divided into 2 disjoint sets such that every edge connects vertices of different sets (no odd length cycles).
explanation: Initialize a `color` array with -1 for all vertices.
For each unvisited vertex, assign `color[start] = 0` and enqueue.
Pop node `u`. For each neighbor `v` of `u`:
If `color[v] == -1`, assign `color[v] = 1 - color[u]` and enqueue `v`.
If `color[v] == color[u]`, graph is NOT bipartite (odd cycle found $\rightarrow$ Return False).
If all nodes colored without conflict, return True.

traceSteps: Pop 3: neighbor 2 is color 0 != color[3] (1). No conflict.
All 4 vertices colored with 2 colors without edge conflicts $\rightarrow$ Graph is Bipartite (True).

algorithms.title: Bellman-Ford Algorithm (Negative Weights & Cycle Detection)
algorithms.summary: Computes shortest paths from a single source vertex to all other vertices in a weighted graph, even with negative edge weights, and detects negative cycles.
explanation: Initialize source distance to zero and all other distances to infinity.
Relax every edge V-1 times.
After V-1 iterations, all shortest simple paths have been considered.
Perform one additional relaxation pass to detect a reachable negative cycle.
Bellman-Ford is slower than Dijkstra but handles negative edges.

algorithms.title: Floyd-Warshall Algorithm (All-Pairs Shortest Path)
algorithms.summary: Computes all-pairs shortest paths in a weighted graph using Dynamic Programming over intermediate nodes k.
explanation: Initialize `dist[i][j]` matrix with edge weights, `0` along diagonal, and `infinity` elsewhere.
Iterate over intermediate vertex `k` from 0 to V-1.
Iterate over all pairs `(i, j)`.
Update: `dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j])`.
After 3 nested loops, `dist[i][j]` holds the shortest distance between any pair of nodes (i, j).

algorithms.title: Prim's Algorithm for Minimum Spanning Tree (MST)
algorithms.summary: Greedy algorithm that builds a Minimum Spanning Tree by growing a tree one vertex at a time using a Min-Heap of connecting edge weights.
explanation: Maintain a `visited` array and a Min-Heap storing `(weight, u)`.
Start with source vertex 0 in Min-Heap with weight 0.
Pop minimum weight edge `(wt, u)` from heap.
If `u` is already visited, skip. Otherwise mark `visited[u] = True` and add `wt` to total MST sum.
Push all edges from `u` to unvisited neighbors into Min-Heap.
Repeat until all V vertices are visited.

traceSteps: Pop (0, 0): visit 0. Add edges (1, 1) & (4, 2) to heap. Heap = [(1, 1), (4, 2)].
Pop (2, 2): visit 2. mst_wt += 2 (3). Add edge (3, 3) to heap. Heap = [(3, 3), (4, 2), (6, 3)].
Pop (3, 3): visit 3. mst_wt += 3 (6). All 4 nodes visited!

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds a Minimum Spanning Tree connecting all vertices with minimum total edge weight.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When designing dense network backbones, cable/piping infrastructure, or electrical grids.
wAnswers.whereUsed: LAN network cable routing, telecommunication grid design, approximation algorithms for TSP.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Greedy choice property guarantees optimal MST in O(E log V) time.

import heapq

def prims_mst(V, adj):
    visited = [False] * V
    min_heap = [(0, 0)] # (wt, u)
    mst_sum = 0
    nodes_visited = 0
    
    while min_heap and nodes_visited < V:
        wt, u = heapq.heappop(min_heap)
        if visited[u]: continue
        visited[u] = True
        mst_sum += wt
        nodes_visited += 1
        for v, weight in adj[u]:
            if not visited[v]:
                heapq.heappush(min_heap, (weight, v))
    return mst_sum

Check if `find(u) != find(v)` (u and v are in different components).

algorithms.title: Tarjan's Algorithm for Bridges & Articulation Points
algorithms.summary: Finds critical edges (Bridges) and critical vertices (Articulation Points) whose removal disconnects an undirected graph using discovery time (`tin`) and lowest reachable time (`low`).
explanation: Maintain `tin[u]` (discovery time) and `low[u]` (lowest discovery time reachable from u).
Perform DFS traversal, updating timer `tin[u] = low[u] = timer++`.
For neighbor `v` of `u` (other than parent):
If `v` is unvisited: DFS(v). Update `low[u] = min(low[u], low[v])`.
Check Bridge condition: If `low[v] > tin[u]`, edge `(u, v)` is a Bridge (Critical Connection)!
If `v` is already visited: Update `low[u] = min(low[u], tin[v])`.

traceSteps: DFS to 2: tin[2]=3, low[2]=3. Neighbor 0 is visited $\rightarrow$ low[2] = min(3, tin[0]) = 1. Backtrack to 1: low[1] = min(2, 1) = 1.
DFS from 1 to 3: tin[3]=4, low[3]=4. Backtrack to 1.
Check Bridge condition for edge (1, 3): low[3] (4) > tin[1] (2) $\rightarrow$ TRUE!
Edge (1, 3) is a Critical Bridge (removing it disconnects vertex 3).

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Identifies single points of failure (vulnerable bridges/nodes) in network topologies.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When auditing network robustness or identifying critical infrastructure routers/servers.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Network vulnerability testing, power grid single-point-of-failure analysis, routing resilience.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: O(V + E) single-pass DFS discovery.

def find_bridges(n, connections):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v in connections:
        adj[u].append(v)
        adj[v].append(u)
        
    tin = [-1] * n
    low = [-1] * n
    timer = 0
    bridges = []
    
    def dfs(u, p):
        nonlocal timer
        tin[u] = low[u] = timer
        timer += 1
        for v in adj[u]:
            if v == p: continue
            if tin[v] != -1:
                low[u] = min(low[u], tin[v])
            else:
                dfs(v, u)
                low[u] = min(low[u], low[v])
                if low[v] > tin[u]:
                    bridges.append([u, v])
                    
    dfs(0, -1)
    return bridges

algorithms.title: Graph Representations & Memory Tradeoffs
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(V + E) conversion, O(1) edge lookup in Matrix, O(deg(u)) in Adj List
algorithms.spaceComplexity: Matrix: O(V^2), Adj List: O(V + E), Edge List: O(E)
algorithms.summary: Master fundamental graph storage formats: Adjacency Matrix (V x V array), Adjacency List (Map/Array of neighbor lists), and Edge List (Array of pairs/triplets). Includes conversion algorithms and memory/lookup tradeoff analysis.
explanation: Graphs can be stored in computer memory using three primary data structures depending on edge density and required operation speeds:

1. Adjacency Matrix: A 2D boolean or integer array matrix[V][V] where matrix[u][v] stores the edge weight or 1 if an edge exists from u to v. Edge lookup O(1), but memory cost O(V^2) regardless of edge count E.
2. Adjacency List: An array of lists or hash map mapping each vertex u to its list of adjacent neighbor nodes (and weights). Memory efficient O(V + E), ideal for sparse graphs.
3. Edge List: A simple array or vector of tuples/structs (u, v, weight). Excellent for edge-centric algorithms like Kruskal's MST and Bellman-Ford, memory cost O(E).
This module provides bidirectional conversion utilities and benchmark metrics between all 3 representations.

traceSteps: Step 1: Input Edge List [(0, 1, 5), (1, 2, 3), (2, 3, 8)] for V=4 Undirected Graph.

Step 2: Build Adjacency Matrix (4x4 initial zeros):
       [0, 5, 0, 0]
       [5, 0, 3, 0]
       [0, 3, 0, 8]
       [0, 0, 8, 0]

Step 4: Query Edge Existence between (1, 2):
       - Matrix lookup: matrix[1][2] -> 3 in O(1)
       - Adj List search: search 2 in list of 1 -> found weight 3 in O(deg(1))=O(2)

Step 5: Memory Footprint Comparison:
       - Matrix: 4x4 = 16 integers
       - Adj List: 4 headers + 6 neighbor nodes = 10 elements
       - Edge List: 3 tuples = 3 elements

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Provides the foundational input parsing, graph instantiation, and data structure conversion mechanisms for all graph algorithms.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use Adjacency Matrix for dense graphs (E ≈ V^2) and quick O(1) edge existence checks. Use Adjacency List for sparse graphs (E << V^2) and BFS/DFS traversals. Use Edge List for Kruskal's MST, Bellman-Ford, and dynamic edge sorting.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Network routing tables, social network graph databases (Neo4j, GraphQL), spatial GIS maps, compiler data flow graphs.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Adjacency List minimizes memory to O(V+E) allowing scale to millions of vertices, whereas Adjacency Matrix leverages CPU cache lines for instant O(1) matrix lookup.

class GraphRepresentation:
    def __init__(self, num_vertices):
        self.V = num_vertices
        self.adj_list = {i: [] for i in range(num_vertices)}
        self.adj_matrix = [[0] * num_vertices for _ in range(num_vertices)]
        self.edge_list = []

    def add_edge(self, u: int, v: int, weight: int = 1, directed: bool = False):
        # 1. Edge List
        self.edge_list.append((u, v, weight))
        # 2. Adjacency Matrix
        self.adj_matrix[u][v] = weight
        if not directed:
            self.adj_matrix[v][u] = weight
        # 3. Adjacency List
        self.adj_list[u].append((v, weight))
        if not directed:
            self.adj_list[v].append((u, weight))

# Example Usage
g = GraphRepresentation(4)
g.add_edge(0, 1, 5)
g.add_edge(1, 2, 3)
g.add_edge(2, 3, 8)
print("Adj List:", g.adj_list)
print("Adj Matrix:", g.adj_matrix)

algorithms.title: Graph Types, Connectivity & Properties Classifier
algorithms.summary: Unified classification framework to analyze graph properties: Directed vs Undirected, Weighted vs Unweighted, Cyclic vs Acyclic (DAG), Connected vs Disconnected components, and Bipartite validation.
explanation: Understanding structural graph properties dictates algorithm selection:
1. Directed vs Undirected: Edges have single-way direction vs symmetric two-way traversal.
2. Weighted vs Unweighted: Edges carry cost values vs uniform unit cost (BFS shortest path applies only on unweighted/equal weight).
3. Cyclic vs Acyclic (DAG): Cyclic graphs contain closed loop paths. Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) enable Topological Sorting and DP over DAGs.
4. Connected vs Disconnected: An undirected graph is connected if every vertex is reachable from every other vertex. Disconnected graphs split into multiple Connected Components.
5. Bipartite Graph: Vertices can be partitioned into two sets U and V such that every edge connects a node in U to a node in V (No odd length cycles).

traceSteps: Step 1: Check Connectivity using BFS/DFS from node 0.
Visited set from 0: {0, 1, 2}. Visited count (3) < V (5) -> Graph is DISCONNECTED.
Step 2: Count Connected Components. Component 1: {0, 1, 2}, Component 2: {3, 4}. Total Components = 2.
Step 3: Cycle Detection on Component 1: DFS detects back-edge from 2 to 0 -> Graph is CYCLIC.
Step 4: Bipartite Check (2-Coloring): Component 1 has cycle (0-1-2-0) of length 3 (Odd Cycle) -> NOT BIPARTITE.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Identifies key topological constraints of a input graph to choose correct algorithms (e.g. Kahn's for DAG, Dijkstra for weighted non-negative, BFS for unweighted).
wAnswers.whenToUse: Run as a pre-processing or validation step whenever entering complex graph workflows.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Dependency resolution systems (pip, npm), bipartite matching in recommendation systems (Users-Items), network vulnerability scanners.

algorithms.title: Connected Components
algorithms.summary: Finds independent connected groups of vertices in an undirected graph using DFS, BFS or DSU.
explanation: Maintain a visited array or set.
Start BFS or DFS from every unvisited vertex.
Every traversal discovers exactly one connected component.
Count how many such traversals are required.
DSU can also maintain the number of components while edges are dynamically added.

traceSteps: Vertex 3 is unvisited, so start another traversal.
Vertex 5 does not exist; therefore there are 2 components.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Determines how many disconnected groups exist and which vertices belong to each group.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use for connectivity and grouping problems.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Networks, islands, social groups and clustering.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: BFS/DFS processes every vertex and edge once.

algorithms.title: Shortest Path in a DAG
algorithms.summary: Finds shortest paths in a directed acyclic graph by processing vertices in topological order.
explanation: Topologically sort the DAG.
Initialize the source distance to zero.
Process vertices in topological order.
Relax outgoing edges of each processed vertex.
Because there are no cycles, every predecessor is processed before its dependent vertices.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Single-source shortest paths in DAGs.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Use when the graph is guaranteed to be a DAG.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Dependency graphs, project planning and critical path analysis.
